skyline.text: Pinker’s parable of two farmers, and why poverty matters more
An economist asks why elites prefer beliefs that cost nothing
The words he left out, and the version protesters held up

brief.head: Staring at the pedals
brief.text: Spotify led Amit Varma to shoegaze, named for guitarists who stared at their effects pedals, and to Galaxie 500, the earlier band of Luna’s Dean Wareham. {046-S01}

brief.head: Stuck in 1992
brief.text: Ajay Shah’s first answer to “what are the two most recent songs that you know?” was *November Rain*. Thinking harder, he found one from 2017 and one from 2018. {046-S02}

brief.head: Instant opinions
brief.text: Amit Varma bristles at people who think about a subject for thirty seconds and tweet a verdict. He has read about it for thirty years, he said. {046-J13}

brief.head: Bootleggers love bans
brief.text: Bruce Yandle’s insight: the moralist demanding a ban and the bootlegger profiting from it want the same thing, so the bootlegger funds the prohibitionist politician. {046-C07}

brief.head: Cronies need not apply
brief.text: Pro-business and pro-market can mean opposite things, Amit Varma said. Businesses ally with the state to keep competitors out; free markets make serving people the only route. {046-C08}

thought.text: Those who signal the most virtue possess the least.
thought.who: Amit Varma, a maxim he often repeats, found especially true of men

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on beliefs that hurt the poor
lead.head: Rich man’s virtue, poor man’s bill
body: It is fashionable, Amit Varma said, to hold opinions that make you feel virtuous while the poor pay. He calls them luxury beliefs, a term from the thinker Rob Henderson, whose definition he read out.
“Luxury beliefs are ideas and opinions that confer status on the upper class while often inflicting costs on the lower classes.” {046-C01}

Varma pictured the believers: elites in air-conditioned living rooms, typing into MacBooks, choosing which luxury headphones to add to the three they already have, and proposing policies that hurt the poor.
His antidote is Gandhi’s test, which both hosts take inspiration from: before any policy, ask first what it does to the poor. In a country as poor as India, Varma said, that is a moral question.
He and Ajay Shah then worked through five such beliefs, mostly from the left, one plainly from the right, and asked why comfortable people hold them.
## Five fashionable mistakes

Socialism, Varma said, is not a word for caring about society. It means a state that owns much of the property and regulates the rest, where freedom is something granted. His lens is consent against coercion, and socialism, he said, is coercion. {046-C02}

Inequality is the wrong target. In a positive-sum world, growth makes the poor richer and the rich richer still, so poverty can fall as inequality rises, as it did after 1991. Would you rather be poor in the USA or in Bangladesh?
Banning victimless crimes, the right’s contribution, hands prostitution, betting and liquor to the underworld, where the rule of law does not reach.
Anti-capitalism scorns the sweatshop that is, for the person working in it, the best option on offer. And price controls throw away the information prices carry, so that scarcity always follows.
## The arithmetic of patience

Shah added numbers. A growth-hostile policy setup, he suggested, gives India about 2 per cent per capita growth; a pro-growth one about 4 per cent. At 2 per cent, incomes take 70 years to quadruple. At 4 per cent, they take 32.
“You think only 200 basis points,” he said, “but there’s a power of compounding.” {046-C05}
Varma put it in people: every one per cent rise in GDP, he said, gets about two million Indians out of poverty.
## Why the comfortable believe

Shah, “a card carrying economist”, asked what the elites are optimising for. Pious views, he suggested, cost nothing once you are rich, buy safety from pitchforks and a populist state, and signal membership of a club.
“To buy a Louis Vuitton is at least expensive,” he said. “Here it’s talk. Talk is free.” {046-C11}
Varma was more generous. Most believers mean well, he said; they signal virtue to themselves as much as to others. Social media then rewards tribes, purity tests and doubling down.
He read from Thomas Sowell’s *The Vision of the Anointed* to show that the habit is old: those who disagree with the prevailing vision are seen as being “not merely in error, but in sin”.
Shah warned business elites who court the strongman that populists have often turned on their rich backers.

Varma closed by recommending Walter Block’s *Defending the Undefendable*, and with some advice. “When it comes to values, be firm on your values,” he said. “When it comes to the facts of the world, the world is deeply complex. Be open, listen to people who disagree with you.” {046-C14}

second.label: Degrowth
second.head: Degrowth on the rocks
second.deck: A partygoer with a single malt meets Amit Varma’s arithmetic of poverty
body: At a party a few days before the recording, Amit Varma met a very successful professional from Hyderabad. Sipping a single malt, the man said he found the word “degrowth” very attractive: India, he felt, had had enough growth. {046-S08}
Varma told him that free speech was fine, but that what he was saying was deeply immoral. Growth, Varma said, is what gets people out of poverty.

Over the last 30 years, he said, every one per cent rise in GDP has got two million Indians out of poverty. {#twomillion} To those who have escaped poverty, it is a number. To Varma, it is two million human beings who can live better lives.

quote.text: Free speech is fine and please say whatever you want, but everything you’re saying is deeply immoral because degrowth hurts the poor.

second.caption: the degrowth enthusiast

third.head: The strongman bites back
body: Business leaders who have skimped on understanding society, Ajay Shah said, often make an intellectual error. They seek out the strongman and collaborate with him, sure that he will deliver the goods. {#strongman}
In Saudi Arabia, MBS led a shakedown of hundreds of rich people. In China, Xi Jinping partly destroyed and partly expropriated the rich. In Russia, Putin went after them.

“Each individual billionaire at some point thought that no, no, no, I’m the insider, I will get special favours by the government, and for some time it seems to work,” Shah said. “But in steady state it didn’t.” {046-S09}
Populist leaders, he said, have often been bad for economic growth in general. The only sustainable path for building firms, in his view, is rule of law and liberal democracy.
third.caption: the strongman’s rich backers

p2.title: Five luxury beliefs
p2.deck: Socialism, inequality, bans, anti-capitalism and price controls: five opinions that flatter the comfortable and hurt the poor

sections.label: Belief One
sections.head: Subjects, not citizens
sections.caption: socialism as coercion
body: Many people hear “socialism” as meaning what is good for society, Amit Varma said, just as populism is confused with popular. It is a deeply toxic word.

His definition is stricter. The state owns a lot of the property and regulates the rest; individual liberty is frowned upon. “You are not a citizen, you are a subject,” he said. Freedom is not the default condition but something granted by the state. {046-C02}

Guests on his podcast *The Seen and the Unseen* who are now in their fifties and sixties, he said, talk fondly of the good old days of socialism. They were elite then and are elite now. Yet socialism, Varma said, kept hundreds of millions poor for decades longer than necessary.
## Marx’s checklist

Ajay Shah suggested an exercise. *The Communist Manifesto* by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels ends with a checklist, a programme for action, and you will be astonished, he said, at how much of it is in modern India. {046-R11}
Communism, Varma replied, is about state coercion and centralising power, and India has seen a lot of that for all its 75-plus years.

~ Why is the idea fashionable again? A young generation, Varma said, feels virtuous at the thought of using the state to do good for society, without caring about the unseen cost, and has not seen the horrors of socialism.

quote.text: I care deeply about consent. It has an absolute value. And socialism is equal to coercion.

sections.label: Belief Two
sections.head: Mind the poverty, not the gap
sections.caption: poverty versus inequality
body: Inequality, Amit Varma argued, is a fashion of the West that India cannot afford while it has poverty to solve. In a zero-sum world, poverty and inequality would move together. In a positive-sum world, growth spreads across the spectrum: the poor get richer, the rich get richer still, and inequality goes up.
That, he said, is what happened after 1991, when hundreds of millions of people came out of poverty. {#liberalisation}
His test: would you rather be poor in the USA, which has greater inequality, or in Bangladesh, which has greater poverty? Everybody, he said, answers the USA. {046-C03}

He drew on the philosopher Harry Frankfurt’s slim book *On Inequality* and its doctrine of sufficiency: define what is enough to live on, and get everyone there. Every Indian government, Varma said, has failed at that. {046-C04}
## Two hundred basis points

Ajay Shah answered the wise senior people who had told him that a little chasing of inequality would do little harm to growth. At 2 per cent per capita growth, he said, incomes double in 35 years; at 4 per cent, in about 16. {#ruleof70}

~ Thirty-two years, the time to quadruple at 4 per cent, is within the planning horizon of the show’s editor, Nomsita, Shah noted. “Thirty-two years later she’ll be younger than you are now,” Varma said.

quote.text: The doctrine of sufficiency is that you define what is enough for a man to live on.

sections.label: Belief Three
sections.head: Ban it, and the mob moves in
sections.caption: victimless crimes
body: The third belief comes from the right, Amit Varma said: prostitution is bad, ban it; betting breeds match-fixing, ban it; alcohol is a social evil, ban it. The bans do not end these trades. They hand them to the underworld, where the cops are paid off and the rule of law does not apply.

In the Netherlands, he said, prostitution is legal, brothels are regulated and advertise openly, sex workers have rights and pay taxes, and the level of crime against them is really low. {#netherlands}

He recalled a talk show hosted by Barkha Dutt on which Kiran Bedi was moralistic about prostitution. Sex workers on the show pushed back: they had got into it willingly, as the best option open to them. {046-S05}
## The bootlegger’s friend
Varma would make betting legal and tax it, as England does, charging the houses rather than the gamblers’ winnings. He wants banks to offer betting the way they offer demat accounts.
He cited the economist Bruce Yandle’s essay on bootleggers and Baptists: the moralist calling for a ban and the bootlegger profiting from it want the same thing. {046-C07}
~ His rule is simple: consenting adults should be free to do whatever they want with each other, as long as they harm no one else. {046-C06}

quote.text: We chose it as a best option open to us, and you let us make our decisions.
quote.who: Sex workers on a TV panel, as recalled by Amit Varma

sections.label: Belief Four
sections.head: Tweeting against capitalism
sections.caption: capitalism and its critics
body: Anti-capitalism, Amit Varma said, is the preserve of both left and right in India. Its believers sit in air-conditioned living rooms, tweeting on a capitalist platform about late capitalism. So many people who rant against Amazon, he added, will also order from Amazon. {#amazon}

Capitalism does turn ugly when it is aligned with power, he conceded. That is crony capitalism, in which a business uses the state to keep competition out. Pro-business and pro-market, he said, can mean opposite things. {046-C08}
In true free markets, the state does little beyond upholding the rule of law, so the only way to make money is by serving people.
## In defence of sweatshops
Sweatshops, Varma said, are amazing. Nobody wants anyone to work in one, but the person who does is there because it is the best option open to them. {046-C09}

Child labour is horrible, he agreed. But blunt bans pushed from Western countries have sent laid-off children into prostitution and crime. Studies by Kaushik Basu, Alan Krueger and Eric Edmonds try to work out the family income above which children stop being sent to work. The long-term solution is growth.
~ The newest fashion he despises is degrowth, which, he said, hurts the poor.

quote.text: Those people chose to work in a sweatshop because it was the best option open to them. Respect their agency, respect their decision.

sections.label: Belief Five
sections.head: No car above Rs 10,000
sections.caption: price controls
body: Amit Varma has spoken about price controls so often, he said, that you could print it on T-shirts. The elite belief runs: this is too expensive, put a price control on it.

He offered a thought experiment. Suppose the government decided that every Indian should have a car, and capped cars at ten thousand rupees. {#tenthousand} He told viewers to pause the video and think, and froze on camera himself. {046-J07}
Cars that cannot be made for that sum, which is all of them, would disappear, he said. The few that exist would sell on the black market, and the industry would die.
## The lost signal
A price, Varma said, signals the scarcities and constraints of the world, and carries an incentive to produce more. Take that information away and scarcity follows. {046-C10}
It is not hypothetical. When stents came under price control a few years back, he tweeted that there would be scarcity. There was, and people died. {#stents}

~ Ban Uber’s surge pricing and there is no car when you must reach a hospital or catch a flight. Such controls follow the *Yes Minister* line he quoted: we must do something, this is something, let’s do it.

quote.text: If you take that information away, you are always going to have scarcities.

sections.label: The diagnosis
sections.head: Virtue at no extra cost
sections.caption: why elites hold luxury beliefs
body: Ajay Shah asked the economist’s question: what are the elites optimising for? The cynical answer is that once you are rich, espousing views that harm the poor costs you nothing.

Pious talk, he suggested, is an old kind of philanthropy that buys safety from folks with pitchforks and from a populist state. {#pitchforks} It also makes you look caring, and it is a cheap way to claim membership of a club. {046-C11}

Timur Kuran’s idea of preference falsification fits too, Shah said: people say what they think will help them get ahead. And all of it needs intellectual soft-headedness, a broad base of doctor-engineer capabilities with very low knowledge of social science and humanities. {#doctors}
## It was always thus

Amit Varma credited most believers with good intentions: we lie to ourselves as much as to others, he said. Social media then rewards tribes and doubling down. At 17 he read Marx and Engels and said silly things; with screenshots, he might never have outgrown them. {046-C12}
But, he said, it was always thus. He read from Thomas Sowell’s *The Vision of the Anointed*, subtitled *Self-Congratulation as a Basis for Social Policy*. {046-C13}
~ Shah closed with a warning for business elites who back the strongman: in Saudi Arabia, China and Russia, the strongman turned on the rich.

quote.text: Those who disagree with the prevailing vision are seen as being not merely in error, but in sin.
quote.who: Thomas Sowell, as read by Amit Varma

side.boxText: Rob Henderson, whom Amit Varma calls a very fine thinker worth following, coined the term “luxury beliefs”. His new book, *Troubled*, is about growing up in foster homes, and Varma recommends it highly. {046-R07}

contQuote.text: Then I feel the incentive to double down on them for ego reasons, and then I become that person. I don’t have that intellectual growth I might otherwise have.

p3.title: Good intentions
p3.deck: Goats, preambles, railway stations and carpets: what each story teaches

stories.start: During the protests against the CAA, and I support the protests
stories.end: so one has to see his full body of work
stories.caption: Indira’s preamble
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the CAA protests and a word in the preamble
stories.head: Whose Constitution is it anyway?
body: During the protests against the CAA, young people across India took to the streets holding up the Preamble of the Constitution. Amit Varma, who supported the protests and opposes the CAA, said it gave him great hope that the young were not apathetic.
It also filled him with despair. {046-S04} The preamble they held up was Indira’s, not Ambedkar’s, and Indira’s has the word “socialist” in it.
He understood why. That version also has the word “secular”, which both hosts believe in, and in today’s times, he said, one could argue it has resonance.

But when the two words were debated in Ambedkar’s time, Varma said, Ambedkar’s answer was no. On “secular”, his reasoning was that if the value is inscribed in every article of the Constitution, there is no need to state it: that is just signalling.
On “socialist”, his answer was that the choice of economic organisation is a question for politics, not the Constitution. Let the political process figure it out.

Ambedkar himself favoured a socialistic form of organisation then, Varma said, but by the 1950s he had changed his mind: “a great thinker who contained multitudes”. The Dalit thinker Chandra Bhan Prasad once told Varma that his heroes are Ambedkar and Adam Smith, and Varma suspects Ambedkar would have approved.
~ Socialism, Varma insisted, is not a harmless word meaning the good of society. {#harmless} It implies state coercion and centralisation, and it was written into the Constitution.
stories.why: Ambedkar, Varma said, was a great thinker who contained multitudes and changed his mind, so one has to see his full body of work. And the fashionable reading of the Constitution quietly carries a word that, in Varma’s view, kept India poor.
stories.postscript: Varma recommends his *The Seen and the Unseen* episodes with Srinath Raghavan on the CAA, and with Chandra Bhan Prasad.

stories.start: let me begin with a story, and this is a story I get
stories.end: That's the end of inequality. Right, and neither of them has a good.
stories.caption: Boris, Igor and the goat
stories.kicker: Amit Varma retells a parable from Steven Pinker
stories.head: Igor’s idea of fairness
body: Two Russian farmers, Boris and Igor, star in a parable Amit Varma took from Steven Pinker’s *Enlightenment Now*. Boris has a goat. Igor does not.
Igor goes to the authority and complains that it is not fair. Asked what he wants done, he says: kill Boris’s goat. {046-S03}
That, Varma said, is the end of inequality. And now neither of them has a goat. He thinks about the story often.

~ Later he returned to it. The redistributor takes Boris’s goat, cuts it in half and gives a half each to Boris and Igor. {#halfgoat} He thinks he has solved both men’s problems, Varma said, and feels virtuous. But tomorrow neither has a goat.
stories.why: How you treat inequality, Varma said, is by killing Boris’s goat: you make both people equally poor. How you treat poverty is through economic growth, which in a poor country will inevitably raise inequality. That, he said, is fine.

stories.start: I wrote a column called The Matunga Racket many years ago
stories.end: It was a really common uh uh racket. And now that shit can't happen.
stories.caption: the Matunga racket
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Section 377 and a police racket
stories.head: Next station: extortion
body: Years ago, Amit Varma wrote a column called *The Matunga Racket*. {046-R20} It described what some cops did while Section 377 made homosexuality effectively illegal in India.
They placed ads on online bulletin boards, asking gay men to come and spend time with them. The men would go to the railway station in question, often Matunga, where plainclothes cops met them.
Then came the extortion. The cops threatened to tell the man’s family, his wife or his father. “And they’d go with him to the ATM, they’d use his card, they’d empty it out.” {046-S06}
~ It was a really common racket, Varma said. Section 377 has since, thankfully, been struck down, and that cannot happen now.
stories.why: A law against a victimless crime, Varma argued, does not just fail: it hands its own enforcers a tool against harmless people. His principle is that consenting adults should be free to do whatever they want, as long as they harm no one else. {046-C06}

stories.start: Oxwam did a study in Bangladesh where thirty thousand children were laid off
stories.end: And the kids' lives can become hell if they continue at all.
stories.caption: the children laid off
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on what happened after the bans
stories.head: Saved from work, lost to worse
body: In Bangladesh, after Western activists complained about alleged sweatshops, 30,000 children were laid off. {#oxfam} Oxfam followed up, Amit Varma said: many of the girls went into prostitution, and many of the boys turned to crime.
In Nepal, a scandal over children making carpets led to 5,000 to 7,000 children being laid off. A UNICEF study found that the girls practically uniformly went into prostitution. {#nepal}
No parent wants a child in a factory, Varma said. Families send children to work because every other option is worse. Good schools need prosperity, and prosperity needs growth.
~ The journalists who write such stories, he said, never follow up. The campaigners feel virtuous and forget, and the children’s lives can become hell.

quote.text: There is no parent in the world who wants a child to work in a factory or a sweatshop.

quiz.q: In Steven Pinker’s parable, what does Igor ask the authority to do about Boris’s goat?
quiz.a: Kill it: inequality ends, and neither farmer has a goat.

quiz.q: Would you rather be poor in the USA or in Bangladesh, and what does the answer show?
quiz.a: The USA: it is more unequal, but poverty, not inequality, is what matters.

quiz.q: At 4 per cent per capita growth, how long do incomes take to quadruple?
quiz.a: About 32 years, by the rule of 70, against 70 years at 2 per cent.

quiz.q: Which two words did Ambedkar decline to put in the preamble, according to Amit Varma?
quiz.a: Secular and socialist: one was mere signalling, the other a question for politics.

quiz.q: What happened when stents were put under price control, according to Varma?
quiz.a: Scarcities of stents, as he had tweeted there would be, and people died.

quiz.q: In Ajay Shah’s analysis, why are luxury beliefs cheaper than a Louis Vuitton?
quiz.a: Because they are only talk, and talk is free, yet they signal club membership.
